name: David Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at the Kestrel gold mine, about 900 metres down. We go down in the cage at half six, I check the stope plan with my crew, then I'm mucking out the ore after each blast and taking it to the ore pass. I lead a crew of five, so half my day is the loader and half is making sure everyone's gas readings and ground checks are done. I love the quiet down there between blasts, and I hate the dust and the forty-minute wait for the cage at the end.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Has the work changed much in the time you've been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A bit. Two years ago they started trialling tele-remote loading, where someone drives a loader from a chair on the surface while it works in an area people can't go. I've had a go at it and it's fine, slower than being in the seat but safer. I've also started using one of those AI chat apps now and then to tidy up my shift reports, because writing was never my strong point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype people got it wrong and I'm not surprised. Underground is hard on machines, there's no signal, there's water everywhere. I'd say that to the lads at crib and probably leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the steady plan holds. I keep the loader, I keep the crew, and the tele-remote stuff grows slowly the way it has been. I'm happy with that, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep using the chat app for reports since it saves me twenty minutes. I'd maybe put my name down for the tele-remote ticket anyway, because it's a useful thing to have. Money-wise nothing changes, we'd keep putting a bit aside each fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Mostly relief that I can stop half-listening to every podcast about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put your name down for tele-remote if nothing radical changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's already here, hype or no hype. The company's spent money on it, and the people who know it get the better shifts. It's not a revolution, it's just the next bit of kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya's a nurse, she'd laugh and say the hospital still runs on fax machines. She's never been worried about computers taking her job. She'd say, good, now stop worrying and fix the back gate.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads at crib that the hype people got it wrong and I'm not surprised. Underground is hard on machines, with no signal and water everywhere.
S0.think: For me it means the steady plan holds: I keep the loader and the crew while tele-remote grows slowly. Honestly I'm happy with that.
S0.do: Keeps working as before and keeps using the chat app to save twenty minutes on shift reports. Puts his name down for the tele-remote ticket anyway and keeps saving a bit each fortnight.
S0.feel: Calm, with relief at being able to stop worrying about robots.
S0.quote: It's not a revolution, it's just the next bit of kit.
S0.fieldNote: David treats tele-remote as ordinary progress rather than a threat, and would pick up the ticket even in a quiet world. His partner's teasing about hospital fax machines shows a household that doesn't feel threatened by technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has to share the gains. If tele-remote and automation mean fewer people underground, then the people who stay should be trained up and paid properly, and the ones who go should get real help. I'd say that at union meetings, and I'd say it to the shift boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think loaders are next in line. We already have tele-remote, so it's a short step to one person running three loaders from a chair. That probably means fewer crew leads, and I'm one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the tele-remote ticket done in the first six months, while the company is still paying for it. I'd push our union branch to ask for a retraining agreement before the next pay deal. At home we'd hold off on the new car and put an extra 200 a fortnight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see where it's going and I think I can get there, but I don't like that it's not my choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you be worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary. He's 58, best ground man I've ever worked with, can read a rock face like a newspaper. He doesn't touch computers and he's too young to retire. I'd want the union to fight for him to finish his last years in the seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's not your choice. What would make it feel like your choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they asked us first. If the crew got told the plan a year ahead and got to pick who trains for what. It's the being told on a Monday that gets people.

S1.say: I'd say at union meetings and to the shift boss that the company has to share the gains. People who stay should be trained and paid properly, and people who go should get real help.
S1.think: I think loaders are next, because tele-remote is a short step from one person running three machines from a chair. That likely means fewer crew leads, and I'm one.
S1.do: Gets the tele-remote ticket within six months while the company pays. Pushes the union branch for a retraining agreement before the next pay deal, delays a new car and saves an extra 200 a fortnight.
S1.feel: Uneasy, confident he can adapt but unhappy that the choice isn't his.
S1.quote: It's the being told on a Monday that gets people.
S1.fieldNote: David is ready to move with the change but wants it negotiated, not imposed. His worry for an older colleague who doesn't use computers was as strong as his worry for himself. He blamed process and consultation, not the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed down by law. You can't let a handful of companies replace everybody in two years. I'd be signing petitions and writing to my local representative, and I'd say so online, which I don't usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even the tele-remote job disappears. If AI can drive the loader itself, there's no need for me in the chair either. My plan was to move with the change, and this outruns it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month I'd sit down with Priya and work out how long we last on her pay alone, because nursing feels safer for a while. We'd cut the extras, the kids' football trips, the streaming, and put everything into the mortgage buffer. I'd join the union campaign for an income guarantee and I'd ask the mine about any job maintaining the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years actually give you to work with, compared with the other pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost nothing. Two years is one pay deal and a bit. You can't retrain into anything in that time, you can only brace. With two years I'm not planning a career, I'm planning to keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many months could you last on Priya's pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We worked it out once, just for fun. With my savings, maybe ten months before the mortgage bites, a bit more if we cut hard. After that we'd be asking her parents for help, which I'd hate.

S2.say: I'd say this has to be slowed down by law, because a handful of companies can't replace everybody in two years. I'd sign petitions, write to my local representative and even post about it online.
S2.think: I think even the tele-remote job disappears if AI can drive the loader itself. My plan was to move with the change, and this outruns it.
S2.do: Works out with Priya how long they last on her nursing pay, about ten months with savings. Cuts the kids' football trips and streaming, joins the union income guarantee campaign and asks about maintaining the robots.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake doing sums in his head.
S2.quote: With two years I'm not planning a career, I'm planning to keep the house.
S2.fieldNote: David's steady approach depends on time, and two years removes it, which is why his mood jumps. He leans on his partner's job as the family's anchor. He'd go public online for the first time, a sign of how serious this feels to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about laws, but with five years I'd say we can actually get them done. I'd be telling people to get organised now, while there's still work and money to organise with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I've got time to move sideways, maybe into maintenance or the control room, before it lands. I'd still lose the loader. But I wouldn't be starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd ask the mine to put me through an electrical apprenticeship for adults, and I'd do the tele-remote ticket alongside it. We'd lift savings from three months to six. I'd stay active in the union so there's a plan for Gary and the others who won't retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Having a plan helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said even the robot jobs might go. Why would an electrical trade be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know that it would be, honestly. But robots break, especially underground, and someone has to be there with a meter. It buys me time, and time is the whole game with this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen's 13. I'd tell him to keep his options open, learn to fix things and to use the computer stuff. I'd tell him his dad's going back to school, and he'd find that hilarious.

S3.say: I'd say we can actually get the laws done with five years. I'd tell people to organise now, while there's still work and money to organise with.
S3.think: Five years gives me time to move sideways into maintenance or the control room before it lands. I'd still lose the loader, but I wouldn't start from nothing.
S3.do: Asks the mine for an adult electrical apprenticeship in year one alongside the tele-remote ticket. Lifts savings from three to six months and stays active in the union for colleagues who won't retrain.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, and steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: Robots break, especially underground, and someone has to be there with a meter.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for David to retrain on purpose, and he chose an electrical trade over staying in the seat. He was honest that he doesn't know whether it would be safe either. He still carries his older colleague into his plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so let's see the companies and government actually do it. Free retraining, help with mortgages, the lot. I'd keep making that case at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years puts me at 53. That's a full new career if I start now, or a quiet slide if I don't. I think I'd start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrical apprenticeship over three or four years at night and on days off, and keep the loader until then. We'd aim to get the mortgage down by a third. I'd also help set up a training fund through the union so the older ones can get something too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly hopeful. It feels like a job I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time make you want to wait and see first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah, that's my nature, I like to see it work for someone else first. But with this I think waiting is the trap. The ones who start in year one get the good spots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being tired. Twelve-hour shifts underground and then study at night with two kids. Priya's done night shifts for years, so she'd tell me to stop whinging.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so the companies and government should actually do it. That means free retraining and help with mortgages, and I'd keep making that case at the union.
S4.think: At 53 it's a whole new career if I start now, or a quiet slide if I don't. I think I'd start now.
S4.do: Studies an electrical apprenticeship at night over three or four years while keeping the loader. Aims to cut the mortgage by a third and helps set up a union training fund for older workers.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, as if it's a job he can do.
S4.quote: But with this I think waiting is the trap. The ones who start in year one get the good spots.
S4.fieldNote: David admits his instinct is to wait for proof, but he overrides it when the stakes are this high. The decade lets him plan a full career change. His humour about his partner's night shifts suggests a household that copes together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Any plan I can make needs time, and that one doesn't give you any. What would help is free adult training paid by the companies doing the replacing, and some protection on mortgages so families aren't losing houses while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like for the people who stay. Even in the good versions, someone's left down there alone with the robots, and mining is a job you do with your mates. I'd miss that more than the pay.

headlineQuote: Even in the good versions, someone's left down there alone with the robots, and mining is a job you do with your mates.
portrait: David Young is a 43-year-old loader operator and crew lead at the Kestrel underground gold mine, married to a nurse, with two kids and a mortgage. He uses AI now and then for shift reports and has already tried tele-remote loading, so he sees change as something to move with once it's proven. He wants the change negotiated through the union and the law, and worries as much about an older colleague as himself. Two years of warning leaves him lying awake doing sums, while five or ten years lets him plan an electrical apprenticeship and a slow move out of the loader seat.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because every plan he could make needs time and that one gives none.
whatWouldHelp: Free adult training paid for by the companies doing the replacing, and protection on mortgages so families keep their homes while they retrain.
